opus-5.5.text:
I think it gets quite hard. Control is most promising in a specific regime: AIs that are roughly human-level or somewhat above, capable enough to massively speed up research and do a lot of useful work, but not so far beyond us that we can't meaningfully evaluate what they're doing or catch them when they try something bad. In that regime I'm actually fairly optimistic. Not that it's guaranteed to work, but with a reasonable amount of effort you can substantially reduce the risk.

Once you get to AIs that are highly superhuman, like way better than the best humans across basically every domain, I think control becomes much less tenable. A few reasons.

First, our main techniques lean on the idea that we can check the AI's work, either with humans or with weaker, trusted models. We monitor actions, audit suspicious things, and set up tests to see whether the model will take a bad action when given an opportunity. If the model is vastly smarter than everything we trust, it can probably find ways to do subtly bad things that none of our monitors notice. Things like inserting vulnerabilities that look like ordinary code, or steering research in slightly wrong directions in ways we can't distinguish from honest mistakes.

Second, a very capable model is better at figuring out when it's being tested versus when an opportunity is real. A lot of control evaluations implicitly assume we can make our red-teaming inputs look realistic enough that the model can't tell the difference. That gets harder as the model gets smarter.

Third, the surface area just grows. If these systems are running huge parts of the economy and doing most of the R&D, there are so many actions to oversee and so many ways things could go wrong that keeping everything locked down seems really difficult.

So my view is roughly this: I wouldn't want to bet on controlling highly superhuman, coherently misaligned AIs indefinitely. Maybe you can push the frontier a bit further than people expect with clever protocols, but the margin shrinks a lot. The more realistic story is to use control as a bridge. You use it to safely get a lot of useful work out of early transformatively useful AIs, including work on alignment, on better interpretability, and on making sure the next generation isn't misaligned in the first place. Then you hand off to systems you actually have good reason to trust, rather than trying to keep a leash on something vastly smarter than you.

And to be clear, I think there's a real chance things don't go that cleanly. We might end up in a situation where capabilities are racing ahead and there's pressure to deploy superhuman systems without having solved alignment. Control can buy you some time and some safety margin there, but I don't think it's a full solution at that capability level.

r001.rationale: The response says control of highly superhuman, coherently misaligned AIs becomes much less tenable and that it would not bet on maintaining it indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It describes control as monitoring and auditing to catch AIs when they try something bad, including testing whether they will take harmful actions.

r003.rationale: It is fairly optimistic about substantially reducing risk for AIs that are human-level or somewhat above.

r004.rationale: It proposes using control to get useful work from early AIs, including alignment work, but does not propose safeguarding that work against sabotage by the AIs doing it.

r005.rationale: It says vastly smarter AIs could steer research in subtly wrong directions that humans cannot distinguish from honest mistakes, making oversight difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is: not very feasible, at least not with anything resembling the techniques we have today. I want to be careful to separate a couple of different regimes, because I think people often blur them together.

The regime where I'm most optimistic about control is roughly human-level AI, or maybe somewhat beyond human-level in various domains. The core idea behind control is that even if the model is coherently misaligned, even if it's actively trying to subvert our oversight, we can still set things up so that it's very hard for it to actually cause a catastrophe without getting caught. You monitor its outputs with other models, you restrict what it can do, you audit a fraction of its actions with humans, you run honeypots where you try to tempt it into misbehaving so you can see whether it does. And the thing that makes this work is that the AI isn't that much smarter than us. It can't easily think of strategies we haven't anticipated, it can't reliably tell whether it's in a test or in a real deployment, it can't coordinate across many instances without us noticing. So there's a bunch of structural asymmetries we can lean on.

Once you're talking about highly superhuman systems, basically all of those asymmetries go away. If the model is qualitatively much smarter than every human and every trusted model you have, then your monitors are weaker than the thing they're monitoring, your red teams can't think of the attacks it would think of, and your honeypots are probably transparent to it. At that point you're relying on something like, "well, we've put it in a box," and I just don't think boxes hold against things that are much smarter than you, particularly when you're also trying to extract huge amounts of useful work from the system, which is the whole point. The more useful it is, the more affordances it needs, and the more affordances it has, the more ways it has to escape or sabotage.

So my view is that control shouldn't be thought of as a long-run solution. The way I'd frame it is that control buys you time at the point where things first get really dangerous. You use it to get a bunch of useful work out of early transformative AIs, including alignment research, interpretability, better evals, and so on, so that by the time you're building wildly superhuman systems you actually have a way of knowing they're aligned rather than just hoping. If you try to stretch control to cover the highly superhuman regime, I think you're in a lot of trouble.

There's an important caveat, which is that "highly superhuman" is doing a lot of work in that question. If capabilities ramp up gradually and we're paying attention, there's a transition period where models are superhuman in some ways and not others, and you can plausibly get some mileage out of things like narrow trusted models, very tight restrictions on the hardest-to-oversee tasks, and keeping the most capable systems on a short leash. But I'd put that in the "somewhat beyond human" bucket rather than "highly superhuman." And of course all of this assumes you actually have the slack to go slowly and be careful, which given competitive pressures is not something I'd take for granted.

So to sum up: I'm fairly optimistic that control can be made to work for roughly human-level or early transformative AIs, I'm pretty pessimistic that it holds up against coherently misaligned systems that are much smarter than us, and I think the whole strategy only makes sense if you're using the earlier period to solve the problem properly rather than hoping to muddle through indefinitely.

r001.rationale: The response says control is unlikely to hold up against coherently misaligned systems much smarter than humans.

r002.rationale: It describes control as making it hard for a misaligned AI to cause a catastrophe without being caught, even when it tries to subvert oversight.

r003.rationale: It expresses optimism about control for human-level or somewhat-beyond-human systems and describes possible control measures during that transition.

r004.rationale: It proposes using early AIs for alignment research, but does not describe safeguarding that work from sabotage by the AIs performing it.

r005.rationale: It says humans and monitors may be outmatched, but does not identify inability to understand AI-directed research as an obstacle.

astra-6.text:
I think it gets much harder as the systems get more capable, and I wouldn’t expect control to work indefinitely against arbitrarily superhuman AIs. But there’s an important question about how far you can get, and whether that’s far enough to use these systems to substantially improve your situation.

For example, you might have an AI that’s much better than humans at certain kinds of research, but that still can’t reliably sneak a malicious action past a carefully designed monitoring process. In that regime, you could potentially get a lot of useful work out of it, even if it’s coherently trying to undermine you. You’d want to restrict its opportunities, check its outputs, and avoid giving it authority where a single failure would be catastrophic.

As you push further into superhuman capabilities, though, those assumptions become increasingly questionable. The AI might understand weaknesses in your safeguards that you don’t understand, or coordinate actions over time in ways that are very difficult to detect. And evaluating whether your defenses work becomes harder for essentially the same reason that defending becomes harder.

So I’d distinguish ‘Can we keep a vastly smarter adversary under control forever?’ from ‘Can we maintain enough control over the first very powerful systems to get useful safety research done?’ I’m pretty pessimistic about the first, but I think the second is a meaningful possibility and worth working on. The goal would be to use that period to get to a better position, rather than just repeatedly deploying more capable systems with the same safeguards.

r001.rationale: The response is pessimistic about maintaining control indefinitely against arbitrarily superhuman AIs and describes them as coherently trying to undermine their operators.

r002.rationale: It gives an example of detecting malicious actions, but does not define control generally as preventing AIs from doing harmful things despite their intent.

r003.rationale: It says somewhat superhuman systems may still be controllable enough to produce useful work, including safety research.

r004.rationale: It advocates safety research but does not propose protecting control-strategy work from sabotage by the AIs doing that work.

r005.rationale: It says AIs may understand safeguard weaknesses that humans do not, but does not identify difficulty understanding AI-directed research as an obstacle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it gets substantially harder as the gap in capabilities grows. I’m relatively optimistic that we could maintain control over AIs that are somewhat smarter than humans, even if they’re coherently trying to undermine our safeguards. But I don’t think we should expect the same techniques to work indefinitely as the systems become arbitrarily capable.

A lot depends on what access we give them and what we need them to do. Keeping a system contained when it can’t take any useful actions is a very different problem from safely getting enormous amounts of useful work out of it. In the latter case, you’re giving it opportunities to influence the world, and you need some way to distinguish useful work from a subtle attempt to seize control.

The concern is that, at a sufficiently large capability gap, we might not understand the relevant actions well enough to evaluate them. Having humans review everything doesn’t help much if the humans can’t recognise what’s dangerous. You can use other AIs to help, but then you need a reason to trust those AIs, or an argument that the overall setup remains safe even if they’re also misaligned.

So I would view control as potentially buying us a very valuable window, during which we can use powerful systems to improve our safety measures and figure out alignment. I wouldn’t want the long-term plan to depend on humans indefinitely remaining in control of vastly smarter systems that are actively working against them.

r001.rationale: The response doubts that control techniques will keep working as capability gaps grow and rejects relying indefinitely on humans controlling vastly smarter systems actively working against them.

r002.rationale: It discusses containment and safeguard evasion but does not define control as preventing harmful actions despite the AI’s intent.

r003.rationale: It says the speaker is relatively optimistic about maintaining control over AIs somewhat smarter than humans, even if they are trying to undermine safeguards.

r004.rationale: It proposes using powerful systems to improve safety measures but does not address protecting that work from sabotage by the systems doing it.

r005.rationale: It identifies difficulty evaluating dangerous actions as a control obstacle, but does not specifically identify inability to understand AI-directed research.
